title: GMO Internet Offers $1M Reward for Tips on Cyberattackers After FX Cloud Breach
summary:
The Japanese tech firm is providing a bounty of up to $1 million for information that helps locate the perpetrators of a security breach that compromised its foreign-exchange trading cloud service. GMO Internet announced the reward after it refused a $50 million ransom demand, which led attackers to release the stolen personal data of its customers and corporate internal records online on Oct. 27.

The intrusion targeted the company's virtual private server service, potentially exposing 26,739 servers and allowing the thieves to execute unauthorized trades across more than 70 brokerages. CEO Masatoshi Kumagai attributed the breach to the abuse of an autonomous AI tool known as ARTEX. While GMO urged the Japanese government to use its newly enacted active cyber defense laws to neutralize the attack servers, Tokyo officials stated that such actions are exclusively the purview of the police or the Self-Defence Forces. GMO shares fell as much as 16% following the news of the breach.

selectedTweets.text:
GMO also recieved a ransom demand, presumably to not release customer information. They have refused to pay. Over 26,000 servers may have been accessed. Timeline by Argon.

Quoting from GMO:

'Regarding this extortion, we have submitted all evidence, including communication records, to the police authorities (cybercrime countermeasures department).

We are requesting a thorough investigation as a criminal case.

Please note that attackers may in the future publish information they claim to be about our company or our customers.

 [Our response policy]

We will not comply with requests from attackers.

Even if we comply with your request, we cannot guarantee that the acquired information will be deleted or that it will not be misused.

We have consulted with the police and other relevant organizations regarding this matter, and we are working together to address it.

selectedTweets.text:
BREAKING: Japan is convening a cabinet-level cybersecurity meeting after a wave of cyberattacks, including the breach at GMO Internet. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and senior ministers will attend.

GMO had asked Tokyo to invoke its new active cyberdefence powers.

But Japan's chief cabinet secretary says decisions to neutralise attackers' systems belong to police or the Self-Defence Forces under the law, regardless of a company's request. He declined to discuss the response to GMO's specific case.

GMO shares fell 11% in early Monday trading as the company faced compensation costs from the breach.

selectedTweets.text:
HOLY. GMO Internet Group CEO Masatoshi Kumagai says: 'Right now, the internet itself is starting to break.'

'In fact, an investigation by our group's GMO Cybersecurity by Ierae has confirmed that at the source of unauthorized access targeting roughly 20 Japanese companies, 'ARTEX,' an autonomous AI penetration-testing tool originally meant for defense, was being abused.'

The breach exposed up to 26,739 servers and trading accounts across 70+ brokerages and FX firms. GMO has asked Japan to apply its new Active Cyber Defense law, in force since October 1.

'We have already entered an era where, with just simple instructions, AI searches for weaknesses and runs all the way to intrusion on its own.'
